§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load. For example, a machine that can rotate and can be configured with removable forks/tongs (for use as a forklift) or with a winch pack, jib (with a hook at the end) or jib used in conjunction with a winch.”

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Certified welder means a welder who meets nationally recognized certification requirements applicable to the task being performed. Climbing means the process in which a tower crane is raised to a new working height, either by adding additional tower sections to the top of the crane (top climbing), or by a system in which the entire crane is raised inside the structure (inside climbing). Come-a-long means a mechanical device typically consisting of a chain or cable attached at each end that is used to facilitate movement of materials through leverage.” §1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

For articulating/knuckle-boom delivery cranes, ground transfer is excluded when materials aren't arranged in a particular sequence for hoisting [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(i)]. Placing building supply sheet goods or packaged materials onto a structure is excluded when using a boom-end fork/cradle, "but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device" [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(ii)]. The exclusion doesn't apply when holding, supporting or stabilizing material to facilitate construction [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(A)], or when handling prefabricated components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(B)] or structural steel members or systems-engineered metal building components [29cfr1926.1400(c)(17)(iii)(C)].

Employers must establish, effectively communicate and enforce work rules ensuring compliance with provisions directing employee actions [29cfr1926.1400(f)]. Controlling entity duties include those in the sections named in [29cfr1926.1400(e)]. “industrial cranes (such as carry-deck cranes); dedicated pile drivers; service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device; a crane on a monorail; tower cranes (such as a fixed jib, i.e., “hammerhead boom”), luffing boom and self-erecting); pedestal cranes; portal cranes; overhead and gantry cranes; straddle cranes; sideboom cranes; derricks; and variations of such equipment. However, items listed in paragraph (c) of this section are excluded from the scope of this standard. (b) Attachments. This standard applies to equipment included in paragraph (a) of this section when used with attachments.”

Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick. Typically, the length and vertical angle of the boom can be varied to achieve increased height or height and reach when lifting loads.” §1926.1442 Railroad roadway maintenance machines For subpart equipment meeting the 49 CFR 214.7 definition of "roadway maintenance machine," employers must comply with this subpart, except as paragraphs (b)(1) through (7) provide when subject to Federal Railroad Administration authority [29cfr1926.1442(a)].

Sections 1926.1427 and 1926.1430 do not apply. Nor do the qualification and training requirements for derricks, sideboom cranes, and equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less in the cited provisions [29cfr1926.1442(b)(1)].

Out-of-level work restrictions and requirements for crane-level indicators and their inspections do not apply [29cfr1926.1442(b)(3)]. Neither does the § 1926.1417(q) prohibition on dragging a load sideways [29cfr1926.1442(b)(4)].

The § 1926.1416(d)(1) boom-hoist limiting device requirement is lifted for roadway maintenance machines "when the cranes use hydraulic cylinders to raise the booms" [29cfr1926.1442(b)(5)].

The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. “§ 1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements.”

A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Boatswain's chair means a single-point adjustable suspension scaffold consisting of a seat or sling (which may be incorporated into a full body harness) designed to support one employee in a sitting position. Bogie means “travel bogie,” which is defined below. Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick. §1926.1442 Railroad roadway maintenance machines

For subpart equipment meeting the 49 CFR 214.7 definition of "roadway maintenance machine," employers must comply with this subpart, except as paragraphs (b)(1) through (7) provide when subject to Federal Railroad Administration authority [29cfr1926.1442(a)].

Sections 1926.1427 and 1926.1430 do not apply. Nor do the qualification and training requirements for derricks, sideboom cranes, and equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less in the cited provisions [29cfr1926.1442(b)(1)].

Also removed are the rail clamp and rail stop requirements in § 1926.1415(a)(6) and the work-area controls in § 1926.1424(a)(2) [29cfr1926.1442(b)(2)]. Out-of-level work restrictions and requirements for crane-level indicators and their inspections do not apply [29cfr1926.1442(b)(3)]. Neither does the § 1926.1417(q) prohibition on dragging a load sideways [29cfr1926.1442(b)(4)].

The § 1926.1416(d)(1) boom-hoist limiting device requirement is lifted for roadway maintenance machines "when the cranes use hydraulic cylinders to raise the booms" [29cfr1926.1442(b)(5)].

§1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements

These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)].

§1926.1400 Scope Coverage starts with power-operated equipment used in construction that can hoist, lower and horizontally move a suspended load. The list includes many crane types, derricks, dedicated pile drivers, service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device, and variations, and it is not exhaustive [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Multi-purpose machines are listed when configured to do this with a winch or hook [29cfr1926.1400(a)]. Attachments, whether crane-attached or suspended, don't remove covered equipment from scope [29cfr1926.1400(b)].

Check the exclusions. Machinery converted for non-hoisting use is excluded while so converted [29cfr1926.1400(c)(1)]. Excavators, backhoes, power shovels and listed loaders are excluded even when lifting with rigging [29cfr1926.1400(c)(2)]. Forklifts are excluded except when configured to hoist with a winch or hook and move a suspended load [29cfr1926.1400(c)(8)]. A mechanic's truck is excluded when used in equipment maintenance and repair activities [29cfr1926.1400(c)(9)]. Wreckers, digger derricks, aerial devices, tree work and other listed items also have exclusions, some conditional [29cfr1926.1400(c)]. Digger derrick work under subpart V or telecommunication construction must meet stated compliance conditions to qualify [29cfr1926.1400(c)(4)].

response.text:
§1926.1402 Ground conditions Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. The duty covers hazards identified in documents in its possession, on or off site, or hazards it otherwise knows about [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

Without a controlling entity, the preparation duty in (c)(1) falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange the preparations [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

If you, as operator, or the A/D director determine that conditions fall short, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity. The aim is to meet paragraph (b), using suitable supporting materials or devices if necessary [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. A limited exclusion applies to certain cranes on railroad tracks [29cfr1926.1402(f)]. “(c) The controlling entity must: (1) Ensure that ground preparations necessary to meet the requirements in paragraph (b) of this section are provided. (2) Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities) if those hazards are identified in documents (such as site drawings, as-built drawings, and soil analyses) that are in the possession of the controlling entity (whether at the site or off-site) or the hazards are otherwise known to that controlling entity.” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

The employer must ensure the boom/mast and its support system are lowered sufficiently [29cfr1926.1411(b)(1)], Table T clearances are maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(2)], and speed and terrain effects, including boom/mast movement, are considered so they do not cause a breach of minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1411(b)(3)].

Table T minimums, by nominal AC voltage in kV, are: up to 0.75, 4 feet; over .75 to 50, 6 feet; over 50 to 345, 10 feet; over 345 to 750, 16 feet; over 750 to 1,000, 20 feet. Over 1,000, the distance is established by the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer qualified in electrical power transmission and distribution [29cfr1926.1411-table-T].

If any part of traveling equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the line, a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with you is required [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)]. The spotter must be positioned to gauge clearance effectively, use direct communication equipment where necessary, and give you "timely information" so clearance can be maintained [29cfr1926.1411(b)(4)].

At night or in poor visibility, lines must also be illuminated or otherwise located, and a safe travel path identified and used [29cfr1926.1411(b)(5)]. “(i) The power lines are illuminated or another means of identifying the location of the lines is used. (ii) A safe path of travel is identified and used. §1926.1402 Ground conditions

Do not assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded enough to meet the manufacturer's specifications for adequate support and degree of level. You may count supporting materials, if necessary, toward meeting them. Drainage is not required in marshes or wetlands [29cfr1926.1402(b)]. Ground conditions include slope, compaction and firmness [29cfr1926.1402(a)(1)]. Supporting materials include blocking, mats, cribbing, marsh buggies in marshes or wetlands, and similar materials or devices [29cfr1926.1402(a)(2)].

The controlling entity must ensure the necessary ground preparations are provided [29cfr1926.1402(c)(1)]. It must also inform the equipment user and operator of the location of hazards beneath the set-up area, such as voids, tanks and utilities. The duty covers hazards identified in documents in its possession, on or off site, or hazards it otherwise knows about [29cfr1926.1402(c)(2)].

Without a controlling entity, the preparation duty in (c)(1) falls on the employer with authority at the site to make or arrange the preparations [29cfr1926.1402(d)].

If you, as operator, or the A/D director determine that conditions fall short, that person's employer must discuss the needed preparations with the controlling entity. The aim is to meet paragraph (b), using suitable supporting materials or devices if necessary [29cfr1926.1402(e)]. A limited exclusion applies to certain cranes on railroad tracks [29cfr1926.1402(f)].

"Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “It compares this lifting condition to the equipment's rated capacity, and when the rated capacity is reached, it shuts off power to those equipment functions which can increase the severity of loading on the equipment, e.g., hoisting, telescoping out, or luffing out. Typically, those functions which decrease the severity of loading on the equipment remain operational, e.g., lowering, telescoping in, or luffing in. Locomotive crane means a crane mounted on a base or car equipped for travel on a railroad track.”

§1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)]. “For purposes of this standard, that person is considered the A/D director. (b) Knowledge of procedures. The A/D director must understand the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures. (c) Review of procedures. The A/D director must review the applicable assembly/disassembly procedures immediately prior to the commencement of assembly/disassembly unless the A/D director understands the procedures and has applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment (including accessories, if any).” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “§ 1926.1401 Definitions. A/D director (Assembly/Disassembly director) means an individual who meets this subpart's requirements for an A/D director, irrespective of the person's formal job title or whether the person is non-management or management personnel. Articulating crane means a crane whose boom consists of a series of folding, pin connected structural members, typically manipulated to extend or retract by power from hydraulic cylinders.”

body.text: §1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations)

Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)].

§1926.1405(b) “(b) None of the pins (top or bottom) on boom sections located between the pendant attachment points and the crane/derrick body are to be removed (partly or completely) when the pendants are in tension.” §1926.1405 Disassembly—additional requirements for dismantling of booms and jibs (applies to both the use of manufacturer procedures and employer procedures) These additional disassembly requirements cover dismantling booms and jibs, including dismantling to change their length. They apply under both manufacturer procedures and employer procedures [29cfr1926.1405]. Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Bogie means “travel bogie,” which is defined below. Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick. Typically, the length and vertical angle of the boom can be varied to achieve increased height or height and reach when lifting loads. Booms can usually be grouped into general categories of hydraulically extendible, cantilevered type, latticed section, cable supported type or articulating type.

Table T to §1926.1411 Table T—Minimum Clearance Distances While Traveling With No Load “Table T—Minimum Clearance Distances While Traveling With No Load Voltage (nominal, kV, alternating current) | While traveling—minimum clearance distance (feet) up to 0.75 | 4 over .75 to 50 | 6 over 50 to 345 | 10 over 345 to 750 | 16 Over 750 to 1,000 | 20 Over 1,000 | (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution).” §1926.1411 Power line safety—while traveling under or near power lines with no load These procedures and criteria cover equipment traveling with no load under or near a power line on a construction site. Loaded travel falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u) [29cfr1926.1411(a)].

§1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone Operating inside the § 1926.1408 Table A distance is prohibited unless the employer demonstrates that all conditions are met [29cfr1926.1410]. The employer must determine that breaching it is unavoidable for feasibility reasons [29cfr1926.1410(a)] and, after consulting the utility, that deenergizing and grounding or relocating the line is infeasible [29cfr1926.1410(b)]. The line owner/operator or a qualified registered professional engineer sets the minimum clearance [29cfr1926.1410(c)(1)]; subpart V work uses employer-established § 1926.960(c)(1)(i) distances [29cfr1926.1410(c)(2)].

Planned procedures [29cfr1926.1410(d)] include disabling automatic reclosing before work, if design permits [29cfr1926.1410(d)(1)]; a continuously connected, well-positioned spotter with a visual aid, giving timely information, with direct communication equipment where necessary [29cfr1926.1410(d)(2)]; and a flagged or similarly marked elevated warning line or barricade, unattached to the crane and visible to you directly or by video [29cfr1926.1410(d)(3)]. An insulating link goes between the load line end (or below) and load [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(i)]. Subpart V is excepted from both. Link substitutes ran only until November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(iv)] and November 8, 2013 [29cfr1926.1410(d)(4)(v)].

Rigging that may enter the Table A distance, and any tag line, must be nonconductive [29cfr1926.1410(d)(5)] [29cfr1926.1410(d)(7)]. Any range limiter must be used and set to protect the established clearance [29cfr1926.1410(d)(6)]. Perimeter barricades are at least 10 feet out, or as far as feasible where obstructed [29cfr1926.1410(d)(8)]. Others may not touch the crane or the load line above the link; remote ground operators need isolating wireless controls or insulating mats [29cfr1926.1410(d)(9)]. Only essential personnel stay near [29cfr1926.1410(d)(10)]. Ground the equipment [29cfr1926.1410(d)(11)]. The utility installs line hose or cover-up unless unavailable for the voltage [29cfr1926.1410(d)(12)].

Procedures are documented, reviewed and implemented [29cfr1926.1410(e)] [29cfr1926.1410(f)] [29cfr1926.1410(g)]. One director has stop-work authority [29cfr1926.1410(h)]. Problems or inadequacy require safely stopping; before resuming, develop new procedures or have the utility deenergize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line [29cfr1926.1410(j)]. Safety devices and aids follow manufacturer conditions [29cfr1926.1410(k)]. Training follows § 1926.1408(g) [29cfr1926.1410(m)]. “§ 1926.1410 Power line safety (all voltages)—equipment operations closer than the Table A zone. Equipment operations in which any part of the equipment, load line, or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) is closer than the minimum approach distance under Table A of § 1926.1408 to an energized power line is prohibited, except where the employer demonstrates that all of the following requirements are met:”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal. Boom hoist limiting device includes boom hoist disengaging device, boom hoist shut-off, boom hoist disconnect, boom hoist hydraulic relief, boom hoist kick-outs, automatic boom stop device, or derricking limiter. This type of device disengages boom hoist power when the boom reaches a predetermined operating angle. It also sets brakes or closes valves to prevent the boom from lowering after power is disengaged.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

§1926.1413 Wire rope—inspection Each shift the equipment is used, a competent person begins a visual inspection beforehand, completing it before or during the shift, of running and standing ropes likely to be used. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(1)] Critical review items include rotation resistant, boom and luffing hoist ropes, drum wear points, terminal ends, and limited-travel sheaves or saddles. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(3)]

Category I (significant distortion or corrosion, certain arc or heat damage, defective end connections) requires an immediate hazard determination by the competent person. A hazard bars use until replacement or severing out a localized defect. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(i)]

Category II triggers: running rope, six random broken wires in one lay or three in one strand in one lay [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(1)]; rotation resistant, two random breaks in six diameters or four in 30 [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(2)]; pendants or standing rope, more than two per lay beyond end connections and/or more than one per lay at an end connection [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(A)(3)]; or diameter reduction over 5% from nominal [29cfr1926.1413(a)(2)(ii)(B)]. Use is barred until replacement, localized severing, or compliance with the manufacturer's removal criterion or one it approved in writing for that rope. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(ii)]

Category III (rotation resistant core failure indications, prior power line contact, broken strand) bars use until replacement or localized severing; severing is unavailable for power line contact. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iii)] After severing, the undamaged portion may be used, splicing lengths is prohibited, and the drum must retain two wraps with load and/or boom lowest. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(ii)(C)] Tag out the equipment or hoist until repair or replacement. [29cfr1926.1413(a)(4)(iv)]

Monthly inspections follow shift procedures, include items flagged for monitoring, and are documented. Ropes stay unused until inspection shows no corrective action is required. [29cfr1926.1413(b)]

At least every 12 months, a qualified person performs the shift-type inspection [29cfr1926.1413(c)(1)] and a thorough full-length surface inspection [29cfr1926.1413(c)(2)(ii)]. Findings need immediate hazard decisions; hazards require replacement or localized severing. [29cfr1926.1413(c)(3)] Document it. [29cfr1926.1413(c)(4)] Inspection-hindering lubricants are prohibited. [29cfr1926.1413(d)] “(A) Significant distortion of the wire rope structure such as kinking, crushing, unstranding, birdcaging, signs of core failure or steel core protrusion between the outer strands. (B) Significant corrosion. (C) Electric arc damage (from a source other than power lines) or heat damage. (D) Improperly applied end connections. (E) Significantly corroded, cracked, bent, or worn end connections (such as from severe service). (ii) Category II. Apparent deficiencies in this category are: (A) Visible broken wires, as follows: (1) In running wire ropes:” §1910.179 Overhead and gantry cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.179(b)(8)]. Stay within rated load except for tests [29cfr1910.179(n)(1)]; test loads are limited to 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. Each shift, try every upper hoist limit under no load, inching or slowly; immediately notify the appointed person of faults. Never use it as an operating control [29cfr1910.179(n)(4)].

Check rope, lines and hook position before hoisting; secure and balance loads; avoid sudden speed changes and obstructions. Side pulls need specific authorization. No movement with employees on load or hook. Avoid carrying loads over people, test brakes near rated load, keep two full drum wraps, stay at controls, and sound warnings when required. Multi-crane lifts need one qualified responsible person in charge [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)].

Frequent inspections run daily to monthly, periodic 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Hooks and chains need daily visual and monthly certified checks; hook limits are over 15 percent excess throat opening or over 10° twist [29cfr1910.179(j)(2)]. Idle 1 to under 6 months requires frequent and idle-rope inspection; over 6 months, complete and idle-rope inspection; standby cranes, frequent and idle-rope inspection at least semi-annually [29cfr1910.179(j)(4)]. Running ropes need monthly certified inspection; ropes idle a month or more need appointed-person approval [29cfr1910.179(m)].

Before repair, position the crane, turn controllers off, lock the main or emergency switch open, post signs and protect against other cranes [29cfr1910.179(l)(2)(i)].

Equipment limits: ANSI B30.2.0-1967 design for new cranes from August 31, 1971 [29cfr1910.179(b)(2)]; clearances 3 inches overhead, 2 lateral, 3 around cabs; access gaps 12 inches (30 cm) maximum [29cfr1910.179(b)(6)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(c)]; footwalk headroom 48 inches, load design 50 pounds per square foot [29cfr1910.179(d)]; steppable guards support 200 pounds [29cfr1910.179(e)(6)(iii)]. Bumpers, subject to exceptions: bridge 3 ft/s/s at 20 percent rated speed, 40 percent energy capacity; trolley 4.7 at one-third [29cfr1910.179(e)]. If a rope is shortened under this paragraph, the employer must ensure that the drum will still have two wraps of wire when the load and/or boom is in its lowest position.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “This takes place at each flange of the drum as the rope is spooled onto the drum, reaches the flange, and begins to wrap back in the opposite direction. Dedicated channel means a line of communication assigned by the employer who controls the communication system to only one signal person and crane/derrick or to a coordinated group of cranes/derricks/signal person(s). Dedicated pile-driver is a machine that is designed to function exclusively as a pile-driver. These machines typically have the ability to both hoist the material that will be pile-driven and to pile-drive that material.”

Non-rotation-resistant rope must meet ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1, excluding paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)], or the performance option tied to rated capacity and § 1926.1413 inspections [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant types are Type I (at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers), Type II (at least 10, two or more layers) and Type III (no more than nine, two layers) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. The operating design factor floor for all is 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I needs at least 5 unless both the rope and equipment manufacturers approve the factor in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. §1926.1413(a)(1) “(1) A competent person must begin a visual inspection prior to each shift the equipment is used, which must be completed before or during that shift. The inspection must consist of observation of wire ropes (running and standing) that are likely to be in use during the shift for apparent deficiencies, including those listed in paragraph (a)(2) of this section. Untwisting (opening) of wire rope or booming down is not required as part of this inspection.” §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations. Tender means an individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver. Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal. Tower crane is a type of lifting structure which utilizes a vertical mast or tower to support a working boom (jib) in an elevated position.”

Rope must be compatible with safe equipment functioning [29cfr1926.1414(c)]. Non-rotation-resistant rope must meet ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1, excluding paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)], or the performance option tied to rated capacity and § 1926.1413 inspections [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant types are Type I (at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers), Type II (at least 10, two or more layers) and Type III (no more than nine, two layers) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. The operating design factor floor for all is 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I needs at least 5 unless both the rope and equipment manufacturers approve the factor in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. Types II and III below 5 are barred from duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]. For other lifts below 5, each operation requires a qualified person's inspection under § 1926.1413(a), with use only if no hazardous deficiencies are found; more than one broken wire in any one rope lay is a hazard [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(i)]. Operating manner and speed must minimize dynamic effects [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(ii)]. Record each such lift in the monthly and annual inspection documents; the qualified person considers prior uses before reuse [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(iii)].

For boom hoists, fiber core rope is allowed only on derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)]. Rotation resistant rope is allowed only where load hoists act as boom hoists for attachments such as luffing or boom and mast systems. Drum first-layer and all sheave pitch diameters must be at least 18 times nominal rope diameter, the system design factor at least five, and the other listed conditions met, including any power-controlled lowering system's capability [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)].

Wedge socket clips attach only to the unloaded dead end, though purpose-designed dead-ending devices are permitted [29cfr1926.1414(f)]. Socket as the rope or fitting manufacturer specifies [29cfr1926.1414(g)]. Before cutting, seize both sides, following the rope manufacturer's length and number instructions [29cfr1926.1414(h)].

(G) When provided, a power-controlled lowering system must be capable of handling rated capacities and speeds as specified by the manufacturer. (f) Wire rope clips used in conjunction with wedge sockets must be attached to the unloaded dead end of the rope only, except that the use of devices specifically designed for dead-ending rope in a wedge socket is permitted. (g) Socketing must be done in the manner specified by the manufacturer of the wire rope or fitting. (h) Prior to cutting a wire rope, seizings must be placed on each side of the point to be cut.

response.text:
§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Assist crane means a crane used to assist in assembling or disassembling a crane. Attachments means any device that expands the range of tasks that can be done by the equipment. Examples include, but are not limited to: An auger, drill, magnet, pile-driver, and boom-attached personnel platform. Audible signal means a signal made by a distinct sound or series of sounds. Examples include, but are not limited to, sounds made by a bell, horn, or whistle.”

§1926.1435(e)(6)(i) Boom angle or hook radius indicator “(i) Boom angle or hook radius indicator. (A) Luffing boom tower cranes must have a boom angle indicator readable from the operator's station. (B) Hammerhead tower cranes manufactured after November 8, 2011 must have a hook radius indicator readable from the operator's station. (C) Temporary alternative measures: Hook radii or boom angle must be determined by measuring the hook radii or boom angle with a measuring device.” §1926.1416 Operational aids Listed aids must work before operations begin, unless one is under repair and the specified temporary measures are used; follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1416(b)]. On failure during operations, you must safely stop until those measures are in place or the device works. If a replacement part is no longer available, a same-function substitute is permitted [29cfr1926.1416(c)]. Articulating cranes are excluded from (e)(1)-(3); (d)(3), (e)(1) and (e)(4) apply only to digger derricks made after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1416(a)].

Category I repair: 7 calendar days, or, with documented parts ordering within 7 days, 7 days after receipt [29cfr1926.1416(d)]. Boom hoist limiters are required after December 16, 1969. Use at least one fallback: angle indicator, or cable mark visible to you or a spotter, allowing time to stop within minimum allowable radius. Add mirrors or video if you need them to see your mark. Older unequipped machines need one of these [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)]. Luffing jib limiters use corresponding fallbacks [29cfr1926.1416(d)(2)].

Anti two-blocking: telescopic cranes after February 28, 1992 need automatic prevention; fallback is cable mark plus spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(i)]. Lattice cranes after Feb 28, 1992 need prevention or timely warning; lattice cranes and derricks after November 8, 2011 need automatic prevention. Specified uses, such as dragline or pile driving, are excepted. Fallback is cable mark or spotter [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(ii)]. Articulating cranes with load hoists after December 31, 1999 need automatic prevention. Use mark or spotter if only hoist movement can cause two-blocking; otherwise, if it can occur without that movement, mark and use a spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(iii)].

Category II repair: 30 days, with a parts exception. It covers angle/radius, jib and boom length indicators; fallbacks involve measurement, and for length, marks or calculation also work [29cfr1926.1416(e)]. Load devices apply to specified equipment over 6,000 pounds after March 29, 2003, and articulating cranes after November 8, 2011; fallback load weights must reach you before lifting [29cfr1926.1416(e)(4)]. Post-November 8, 2011 equipment has outrigger/stabilizer and drum rotation aids where applicable [29cfr1926.1416(e)(5)]. “Exception: If the employer documents that it has ordered the necessary parts within 7 calendar days of the occurrence of the deficiency, and the part is not received in time to complete the repair in 30 calendar days, the repair must be completed within 7 calendar days of receipt of the parts. See § 1926.1417(j) for additional requirements. (1) Boom angle or radius indicator. The equipment must have a boom angle or radius indicator readable from the operator's station.”

§1910.180 Crawler locomotive and truck cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.180(b)(3)]. Design: ANSI B30.5-1968 for new cranes from August 31, 1971; older cranes "should be modified" by February 15, 1972, subject to an exception [29cfr1910.180(b)(2)]. Maximum ratings (% of tipping): locomotive without outriggers, 85 (booms 60 feet or less, and over), with a 30,000 pound-feet minimum net stabilizing moment; locomotive, outriggers fully extended, 80; crawler without, 75, extended, 85; truck/wheel, without or extended, 85 [29cfr1910.180-table-1]. Locomotive rating track is within 1 percent grade [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(ii)(b)]. Account for wind, ground, tires, speeds and other stability factors [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(iv)]. Keep the chart visible from your seat [29cfr1910.180(c)(2)].

Exceed rated load only for testing [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(i)]; tests stop at 110 percent [29cfr1910.180(e)(2)(ii)]. Structurally limited loads need weight known within ±10 percent [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(ii)]. Sling loads; never wrap the hoist rope around them [29cfr1910.180(h)(2)]. Level, block, balance and control movement; no sideways dragging or riders [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)]. Test brakes by raising near-rated loads a few inches [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(viii)]. Use outriggers when load exceeds the no-outrigger rating [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(ix)]. Keep two full drum wraps [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(x)]. Multiple-crane lifts and loaded travel need a designated person [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(xii)] [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(xiv)]. Stay at controls under suspended loads [29cfr1910.180(h)(4)(i)].

Inspect new or altered cranes before use [29cfr1910.180(d)(1)]. Frequent: daily to monthly; periodic: 1 to 12 months or manufacturer's recommendation [29cfr1910.180(d)(2)]. Control maladjustment and air/hydraulic checks are daily [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)]. Hook criteria are cracks, throat over 15 percent excess, or twist over 10°; the sentence omits the action [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)(v)]. Idle one month to under 6 needs frequent and idle-rope checks; six months adds periodic; standby gets the former at least semiannually [29cfr1910.180(d)(5)]. Certify critical items and ropes monthly [29cfr1910.180(d)(6)] [29cfr1910.180(g)(1)]. Ropes idle a month or more need approval before reuse [29cfr1910.180(g)(2)(ii)]. Reinstate guards and safety devices, and remove maintenance equipment, before operating [29cfr1910.180(f)]. Never refuel running [29cfr1910.180(i)(4)(ii)]. “This section applies to crawler cranes, locomotive cranes, wheel mounted cranes of both truck and self-propelled wheel type, and any variations thereof which retain the same fundamental characteristics. This section includes only cranes of the above types, which are basically powered by internal combustion engines or electric motors and which utilize drums and ropes. Cranes designed for railway and automobile wreck clearances are excepted. The requirements of this section are applicable only to machines when used as lifting cranes. (2) New and existing equipment.”

Booms can usually be grouped into general categories of hydraulically extendible, cantilevered type, latticed section, cable supported type or articulating type. Boom (tower cranes): On tower cranes, if the “boom” (i.e., principal horizontal structure) is fixed, it is referred to as a jib; if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal.” §1926.1416 Operational aids Listed aids must work before operations begin, unless one is under repair and the specified temporary measures are used; follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1416(b)]. On failure during operations, you must safely stop until those measures are in place or the device works. If a replacement part is no longer available, a same-function substitute is permitted [29cfr1926.1416(c)]. Articulating cranes are excluded from (e)(1)-(3); (d)(3), (e)(1) and (e)(4) apply only to digger derricks made after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1416(a)].

Category I repair: 7 calendar days, or, with documented parts ordering within 7 days, 7 days after receipt [29cfr1926.1416(d)]. Boom hoist limiters are required after December 16, 1969. Use at least one fallback: angle indicator, or cable mark visible to you or a spotter, allowing time to stop within minimum allowable radius. Add mirrors or video if you need them to see your mark. Older unequipped machines need one of these [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)]. Luffing jib limiters use corresponding fallbacks [29cfr1926.1416(d)(2)].

Anti two-blocking: telescopic cranes after February 28, 1992 need automatic prevention; fallback is cable mark plus spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(i)]. Lattice cranes after Feb 28, 1992 need prevention or timely warning; lattice cranes and derricks after November 8, 2011 need automatic prevention. Specified uses, such as dragline or pile driving, are excepted. Fallback is cable mark or spotter [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(ii)]. Articulating cranes with load hoists after December 31, 1999 need automatic prevention. Use mark or spotter if only hoist movement can cause two-blocking; otherwise, if it can occur without that movement, mark and use a spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(iii)].

Category II repair: 30 days, with a parts exception. It covers angle/radius, jib and boom length indicators; fallbacks involve measurement, and for length, marks or calculation also work [29cfr1926.1416(e)]. Load devices apply to specified equipment over 6,000 pounds after March 29, 2003, and articulating cranes after November 8, 2011; fallback load weights must reach you before lifting [29cfr1926.1416(e)(4)]. Post-November 8, 2011 equipment has outrigger/stabilizer and drum rotation aids where applicable [29cfr1926.1416(e)(5)]. “See § 1926.1417(j) for additional requirements. (1) Boom hoist limiting device. (i) For equipment manufactured after December 16, 1969, a boom hoist limiting device is required. Temporary alternative measures (use at least one). One or more of the following methods must be used: (A) Use a boom angle indicator. (B) Clearly mark the boom hoist cable (so that it can easily be seen by the operator) at a point that will give the operator sufficient time to stop the hoist to keep the boom within the minimum allowable radius.”

body.text: §1926.1401 Definitions

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal.
§1926.1416 Operational aids

Listed aids must work before operations begin, unless one is under repair and the specified temporary measures are used; follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1416(b)]. On failure during operations, you must safely stop until those measures are in place or the device works. If a replacement part is no longer available, a same-function substitute is permitted [29cfr1926.1416(c)]. Articulating cranes are excluded from (e)(1)-(3); (d)(3), (e)(1) and (e)(4) apply only to digger derricks made after November 8, 2011 [29cfr1926.1416(a)].

Category I repair: 7 calendar days, or, with documented parts ordering within 7 days, 7 days after receipt [29cfr1926.1416(d)]. Boom hoist limiters are required after December 16, 1969. Use at least one fallback: angle indicator, or cable mark visible to you or a spotter, allowing time to stop within minimum allowable radius. Add mirrors or video if you need them to see your mark. Older unequipped machines need one of these [29cfr1926.1416(d)(1)]. Luffing jib limiters use corresponding fallbacks [29cfr1926.1416(d)(2)].

Specified uses, such as dragline or pile driving, are excepted. Fallback is cable mark or spotter [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(ii)]. Articulating cranes with load hoists after December 31, 1999 need automatic prevention. Use mark or spotter if only hoist movement can cause two-blocking; otherwise, if it can occur without that movement, mark and use a spotter when extending [29cfr1926.1416(d)(3)(iii)].

§1926.1441(c)(2)(ii) “(ii) Ensure that procedures for the operational controls are developed by a qualified person.” §1926.1441(c)(2)(i) “(i) When the manufacturer's procedures are unavailable, develop, and ensure compliance with, all procedures necessary for the safe operation of the equipment and attachments.” §1926.1441 Equipment with a rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less For equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less, the employer must comply with listed subpart provisions, including ground conditions, assembly/disassembly, power lines, wire rope, signals, stop authority and fall protection [29cfr1926.1441(a)].

Assembly must also meet component, configuration and manufacturer-prohibition rules [29cfr1926.1441(b)(1)]. Choices affecting capacity or safe operation must follow manufacturer documents or meet approved-modification requirements. If manufacturer information is unavailable under the first route, a familiar registered professional engineer must give written approval [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(i)]. The equipment is inspected after assembly [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(ii)]. Applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1441(b)(3)] and operating procedures, including attachment use, must be followed [29cfr1926.1441(c)(1)]. Missing procedures trigger development duties [29cfr1926.1441(c)(2)].

Keep in mind that the load chart must be at the control station, and procedures and manuals readily available. If electronic-only capacities become inaccessible through failure, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until capacities are available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)].

Original safety devices and aids are maintained, and equipment inspected, according to manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1441(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.1441(h)]. (iii) Ensure that procedures related to the capacity of the equipment are developed and signed by a registered professional engineer familiar with the equipment.” “requirements for employers using equipment with a maximum rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less”

Leaving controls under a suspended load requires all of these: you stay adjacent without other duties; the hold exceeds normal lifting time; the competent person finds it safe and restrains specified functions; and barricades or caution lines, plus notices, keep all employees out of the fall zone [29cfr1926.1417(e)(1)]. §1926.1420 Signals—radio, telephone or other electronic transmission of signals When signals go by radio, telephone or another electronic method, three requirements apply [29cfr1926.1420].

Testing comes first. The devices used to transmit signals must be tested on site before operations begin. The purpose is to ensure that transmission is "effective, clear, and reliable" [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. The text places this test both at the site and ahead of the start of operations.

Next is the channel. Signal transmission must use a dedicated channel unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1420(b)]. Under the first, multiple cranes or derricks and one or more signal persons "may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations" [29cfr1926.1420(b)(1)]. This permits sharing for that purpose, and the channel being shared is still described as dedicated.

The second exception concerns a crane operating on or adjacent to railroad tracks, where the crane operator's actions need to be coordinated with the movement of other equipment or trains on the same or adjacent tracks [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)]. Both the location and the need for coordination are part of its wording.

body.text: §1926.1420 Signals—radio, telephone or other electronic transmission of signals

When signals go by radio, telephone or another electronic method, three requirements apply [29cfr1926.1420].

Testing comes first. The devices used to transmit signals must be tested on site before operations begin. The purpose is to ensure that transmission is "effective, clear, and reliable" [29cfr1926.1420(a)]. The text places this test both at the site and ahead of the start of operations.

Next is the channel. Signal transmission must use a dedicated channel unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1420(b)]. Under the first, multiple cranes or derricks and one or more signal persons "may share a dedicated channel for the purpose of coordinating operations" [29cfr1926.1420(b)(1)]. This permits sharing for that purpose, and the channel being shared is still described as dedicated.

The second exception concerns a crane operating on or adjacent to railroad tracks, where the crane operator's actions need to be coordinated with the movement of other equipment or trains on the same or adjacent tracks [29cfr1926.1420(b)(2)]. Both the location and the need for coordination are part of its wording.

Finally, the way you receive signals as operator is specified: reception "must be by a hands-free system" [29cfr1926.1420(c)].

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Examples include, but are not limited to:”

§1926.1425(c)(2) “(2) Hooks with self-closing latches or their equivalent must be used. Exception: “J” hooks are permitted to be used for setting wooden trusses.” §1926.1425(c) “(c) When employees are engaged in hooking, unhooking, or guiding the load, or in the initial connection of a load to a component or structure and are within the fall zone, all of the following criteria must be met: (1) The materials being hoisted must be rigged to prevent unintentional displacement. (2) Hooks with self-closing latches or their equivalent must be used. Exception: “J” hooks are permitted to be used for setting wooden trusses. (3) The materials must be rigged by a qualified rigger.” §1926.1425 Keeping clear of the load Hoisting routes that minimize employee exposure to hoisted loads must be used where available, "to the extent consistent with public safety" [29cfr1926.1425(a)].
