§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Standard Method means the protocol in appendix A of this subpart for hand signals. Such as means “such as, but not limited to.” Superstructure: See Upperworks. Tagline means a rope (usually fiber) attached to a lifted load for purposes of controlling load spinning and pendular motions or used to stabilize a bucket or magnet during material handling operations. Tender means an individual responsible for monitoring and communicating with a diver. Tilt up or tilt down operation means raising/lowering a load from the horizontal to vertical or vertical to horizontal.”

Qualified evaluator (not a third party) means a person employed by the signal person's employer who has demonstrated that he/she is competent in accurately assessing whether individuals meet the Qualification Requirements in this subpart for a signal person.” §1926.1428 Signal person qualifications The signal person's employer must ensure each signal person meets the Qualification Requirements before giving any signals, using Option (1) or Option (2) [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. Option (1) relies on documentation from a third party qualified evaluator showing the person meets them [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. Under Option (2), the employer's qualified evaluator assesses the person, determines that the requirements are met and documents that determination. This assessment "is not portable": other employers may not use it to meet this section [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

Under either option, the documentation must be available at the site while the employer employs the signal person. It must specify each type of signaling, such as hand or radio signals, for which the person qualifies [29cfr1926.1428(a)(3)].

These are demonstrated through an oral or written test and a practical test [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

§1926.1428 Signal person qualifications

The signal person's employer must ensure each signal person meets the Qualification Requirements before giving any signals, using Option (1) or Option (2) [29cfr1926.1428(a)]. Option (1) relies on documentation from a third party qualified evaluator showing the person meets them [29cfr1926.1428(a)(1)]. Under Option (2), the employer's qualified evaluator assesses the person, determines that the requirements are met and documents that determination. This assessment "is not portable": other employers may not use it to meet this section [29cfr1926.1428(a)(2)].

Under either option, the documentation must be available at the site while the employer employs the signal person. It must specify each type of signaling, such as hand or radio signals, for which the person qualifies [29cfr1926.1428(a)(3)].

Qualification covers knowing the signals used, including the Standard Method if hand signals are used [29cfr1926.1428(c)(1)]; competence in applying them [29cfr1926.1428(c)(2)]; a basic understanding of equipment operation and limitations, including swing and stopping dynamics and boom deflection [29cfr1926.1428(c)(3)]; and the relevant requirements of §§ 1926.1419 through 1926.1422 and 1926.1428 [29cfr1926.1428(c)(4)]. These are demonstrated through an oral or written test and a practical test [29cfr1926.1428(c)(5)].

If later actions indicate a signal person does not qualify, the employer must not allow continued signaling work until retraining and a confirming re-assessment under paragraph (a) [29cfr1926.1428(b)].

§1926.1408 Power line safety (up to 350 kV)—equipment operations Before operating, the employer must identify the work zone: demarcated boundaries you are prohibited from passing, or 360 degrees out to maximum working radius [29cfr1926.1408(a)(1)]. If equipment, load line or load (with rigging and accessories) could get within 20 feet of a line at that radius, one option applies: utility-confirmed deenergizing with visible worksite grounding, 20-foot clearance, or Table A clearance [29cfr1926.1408(a)(2)]. Table A (AC, nominal kV): up to 50, 10 feet; over 50 to 200, 15; over 200 to 350, 20; over 350 to 500, 25; over 500 to 750, 35; over 750 to 1,000, 45; over 1,000, set by the utility or a qualified registered professional engineer. Upper values are inclusive [29cfr1926.1408-table-A]. Requested voltage information is due from the utility within two working days [29cfr1926.1408(c)].

Where encroachment precautions are required, there must be a planning meeting, non-conductive tag lines if used, and a flagged or high-visibility warning line, barricade or sign line in your view at the applicable distance [29cfr1926.1408(b)]. At least one measure is also required: proximity alarm, dedicated spotter, automatic warning device, automatic range limiter, or insulating link/device; subpart V work is excepted from this [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)] [29cfr1926.1408(b)(5)]. If you cannot see the warning line, a dedicated spotter is required plus one of the other four [29cfr1926.1408(b)(3)]. Spotters need continuous contact, a visual aid, effective positioning, direct communication equipment where necessary, and must give timely information [29cfr1926.1408(b)(4)(ii)].

Operating below lines requires confirmed deenergizing and worksite grounding unless an exception applies [29cfr1926.1408(d)]. Presume lines energized [29cfr1926.1408(e)]. Near transmitter towers where charge could be induced, deenergize the transmitter, or ground the equipment and use only non-conductive tag lines if any [29cfr1926.1408(f)]. Training covers contact procedures, line presumptions, device limitations and grounding [29cfr1926.1408(g)(1)]. Safety devices, aids and contact-prevention means used for compliance must meet manufacturer procedures and conditions [29cfr1926.1408(h)]. “Table A—Minimum Clearance Distances Voltage (nominal, kV, alternating current) | Minimum clearance distance (feet) up to 50 | 10 over 50 to 200 | 15 over 200 to 350 | 20 over 350 to 500 | 25 over 500 to 750 | 35 over 750 to 1,000 | 45 over 1,000 | (as established by the utility owner/operator or registered professional engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution).”

§1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Flange points are points of contact between rope and drum flange where the rope changes layers. Floating cranes/derricks means equipment designed by the manufacturer (or employer) for marine use by permanent attachment to a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation. For example means “one example, although there are others.” Free fall (of the load line) means that only the brake is used to regulate the descent of the load line (the drive mechanism is not used to drive the load down faster or retard its lowering).”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

Boatswain's chair means a single-point adjustable suspension scaffold consisting of a seat or sling (which may be incorporated into a full body harness) designed to support one employee in a sitting position. Bogie means “travel bogie,” which is defined below. Boom (equipment other than tower crane) means an inclined spar, strut, or other long structural member which supports the upper hoisting tackle on a crane or derrick.” §1926.1435 Tower cranes Subpart rules apply unless specified otherwise [29cfr1926.1435(a)], including §§1926.1403–.1406 for erecting, climbing and dismantling, except as otherwise specified [29cfr1926.1435(b)(1)]. Self-erecting cranes have an entry restriction until locked and cleared, with a manufacturer-instruction exception [29cfr1926.1435(b)(2)]. Foundations need manufacturer or registered professional engineer (RPE) design [29cfr1926.1435(b)(3)]. The A/D director addresses §1926.1404(h)(1)–(9), installation per design, backward stability and wind [29cfr1926.1435(b)(4)]. Plumb defaults to at least 1:500 (approximately 1 inch in 40 feet) absent a manufacturer tolerance; a qualified person verifies it [29cfr1926.1435(b)(5)]. Multiple hammerheads may overfly but not be able to contact another's structure [29cfr1926.1435(b)(6)]. Climbing [29cfr1926.1435(b)(7)], counterweight/ballast [29cfr1926.1435(b)(8)] and signs [29cfr1926.1435(c)] have manufacturer or RPE controls.

On failure, stop safely; the crane leaves service until repair, without alternative measures [29cfr1926.1435(d)(3)]. For a failed operational aid, stop until temporary measures are in place or it works [29cfr1926.1435(e)(4)]. Follow any more protective manufacturer measures [29cfr1926.1435(e)(3)].

Category I covers travel, boom, two-block, drum, moment and line-pull limits plus boom-drum locking. Repair within 7 calendar days; if parts are documented as ordered within 7, repair within 7 of receipt [29cfr1926.1435(e)(5)]. Alternatives include marks, spotters, radius and load determination, capacity checks or manual setting. Trolley Option B and rail travel require communicating spotters within 10 feet of end stops. Post-November 8, 2011 cranes need protection for the last 2 drum wraps.

Category II covers angle/radius, deceleration, wind and load indicators. The limit is 30 days; with parts documented as ordered within 7 but arriving too late, 7 from receipt [29cfr1926.1435(e)(6)]. The post-November 8, 2011 condition applies to hammerhead radius and load indicators. Alternatives include measurements, cab notices, wind information or estimates, and load-weight determination.

Inspections include pre-erection, post-erection load testing, monthly and annual items [29cfr1926.1435(f)]. “The equipment must be taken out of service, and operations must not resume until the device is again working properly. See § 1926.1417(f). Alternative measures are not permitted to be used. (e) Operational aids. (1) Section 1926.1416 does not apply to tower cranes. (2) The devices listed in this section (“operational aids”) are required on all tower cranes covered by this subpart, unless otherwise specified. (3) Operations must not begin unless the operational aids are in proper working order, except where the employer meets the specified temporary alternative measures.”

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. response.text:
§1926.1437 Floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. §1926.1441(d)(2) Anti two-blocking “(2) Anti two-blocking. The employer must ensure that equipment covered by this section manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 have either an anti two-block device that meets the requirements of § 1926.1416(d)(3), or is designed so that, in the event of a two-block situation, no damage or load failure will occur (for example, by using a power unit that stalls in response to a two-block situation).” §1926.1441 Equipment with a rated hoisting/lifting capacity of 2,000 pounds or less For equipment rated at 2,000 pounds or less, the employer must comply with listed subpart provisions, including ground conditions, assembly/disassembly, power lines, wire rope, signals, stop authority and fall protection [29cfr1926.1441(a)].

Assembly must also meet component, configuration and manufacturer-prohibition rules [29cfr1926.1441(b)(1)]. Choices affecting capacity or safe operation must follow manufacturer documents or meet approved-modification requirements. If manufacturer information is unavailable under the first route, a familiar registered professional engineer must give written approval [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(i)]. The equipment is inspected after assembly [29cfr1926.1441(b)(2)(ii)]. Applicable manufacturer prohibitions [29cfr1926.1441(b)(3)] and operating procedures, including attachment use, must be followed [29cfr1926.1441(c)(1)]. Missing procedures trigger development duties [29cfr1926.1441(c)(2)].

Keep in mind that the load chart must be at the control station, and procedures and manuals readily available. If electronic-only capacities become inaccessible through failure, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until capacities are available [29cfr1926.1441(c)(3)].

Original safety devices and aids are maintained, and equipment inspected, according to manufacturer procedures [29cfr1926.1441(d)(1)] [29cfr1926.1441(h)]. Equipment manufactured more than one year after November 8, 2010 needs compliant anti two-block protection or a protective design [29cfr1926.1441(d)(2)]. Operators need pre-operation training [29cfr1926.1441(e)], and signal persons need signal training [29cfr1926.1441(f)]. Hoisting personnel is prohibited [29cfr1926.1441(j)]. A qualified engineer must design the equipment [29cfr1926.1441(k)]. “(iii) When rated capacities are available at the control station only in electronic form and a failure occurs that makes the rated capacities inaccessible, the operator immediately ceases operations or follows safe shut-down procedures until the rated capacities (in electronic or other form) are available. (d) Safety devices and operational aids. (1) The employer must ensure that safety devices and operational aids that are part of the original equipment are maintained in accordance with manufacturer procedures. §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Boom (tower cranes): On tower cranes, if the “boom” (i.e., principal horizontal structure) is fixed, it is referred to as a jib; if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal. Boom hoist limiting device includes boom hoist disengaging device, boom hoist shut-off, boom hoist disconnect, boom hoist hydraulic relief, boom hoist kick-outs, automatic boom stop device, or derricking limiter.”

§1926.1417 Operation Follow applicable manufacturer procedures; where unavailable, the employer's substitutes apply [29cfr1926.1417(a)] [29cfr1926.1417(b)(1)]. Keep procedures and load charts in the cab; if electronic-only capacities become inaccessible, cease operations or follow safe shut-down until available [29cfr1926.1417(c)]. Avoid diverting activities while operating [29cfr1926.1417(d)].

Leaving controls under a suspended load requires all of these: you stay adjacent without other duties; the hold exceeds normal lifting time; the competent person finds it safe and restrains specified functions; and barricades or caution lines, plus notices, keep all employees out of the fall zone [29cfr1926.1417(e)(1)]. Negligible-weight working gear not over an entrance or exit is excepted [29cfr1926.1417(e)(2)].

With warning signs, don't start or activate the affected control until an authorized person removes the sign, or you verify nobody is servicing, working on or dangerously positioned on the machine, and it is repaired and working properly [29cfr1926.1417(f)(2)]. Before engine start, verify control positions and clear personnel [29cfr1926.1417(g)]. Promptly report needed repairs in writing to the designated person and any next-shift operator [29cfr1926.1417(j)(1)].

Stay within rated capacity [29cfr1926.1417(o)(1)]. Verify load weight through recognized or equally reliable information, provided before the lift on request. Alternatively, begin hoisting with a listed device to check whether it exceeds 75 percent of maximum rated capacity at the longest radius to be used; if so, don't proceed until weight is verified by the first method [29cfr1926.1417(o)(3)].

At 90% or more of maximum line pull, lift a few inches and apply brakes each time; in duty-cycle or repetitive lifts all at that level, test only the first [29cfr1926.1417(s)]. Keep at least two full wraps on drums [29cfr1926.1417(t)].

No obstruction contact, side dragging or pulling, or front-area lifts on wheeled equipment unless the manufacturer permits [29cfr1926.1417(p)] [29cfr1926.1417(q)] [29cfr1926.1417(r)]. Control swing and load rotation, adjust brakes properly, and obey anyone's stop signal [29cfr1926.1417(v)] [29cfr1926.1417(w)] [29cfr1926.1417(x)] [29cfr1926.1417(y)]. Travel, slack-rope, wind/ice/snow, locomotive-crane and counterweight conditions also apply [29cfr1926.1417(u)] [29cfr1926.1417(m)] [29cfr1926.1417(n)] [29cfr1926.1417(z)] [29cfr1926.1417(aa)]. Safety devices and aids don't replace judgment [29cfr1926.1417(k)]. “(p) The boom or other parts of the equipment must not contact any obstruction. (q) The equipment must not be used to drag or pull loads sideways. (r) On wheel-mounted equipment, no loads must be lifted over the front area, except as permitted by the manufacturer. (s) The operator must test the brakes each time a load that is 90% or more of the maximum line pull is handled by lifting the load a few inches and applying the brakes. In duty cycle and repetitive lifts where each lift is 90% or more of the maximum line pull, this requirement applies to the first lift but not to successive lifts.” §1926.1404 Assembly/Disassembly—general requirements (applies to all assembly and disassembly operations) Assembly/disassembly is directed by the A/D director: a competent and qualified person, or a competent person assisted by qualified persons. A lone worker must be both [29cfr1926.1404(a)]. The director must understand the procedures [29cfr1926.1404(b)], reviewing them immediately beforehand unless already understanding and having applied them to the same equipment type and configuration [29cfr1926.1404(c)]. Crew must understand tasks, hazards and locations to avoid before work, task changes or additions of personnel [29cfr1926.1404(d)].

Crew must notify you before entering covered out-of-view locations where equipment or load movement could injure them [29cfr1926.1404(e)(1)]. If you know someone went there, move no part or load until the pre-arranged communication system confirms they are safe [29cfr1926.1404(e)(2)]. Nobody may be under components during pin removal unless the employer demonstrates site constraints require it; the director must then minimize movement risk and exposure [29cfr1926.1404(f)].

Rated capacity limits apply in all phases [29cfr1926.1404(g)]. The director addresses ground, blocking, assist crane loads (verified beforehand), pick points, center of gravity, stability at pin removal, snagging, counterweights, backward stability and weather [29cfr1926.1404(h)]. Test the boom hoist brake each time before relying on it; if insufficient, use another specified protection against boom movement [29cfr1926.1404(h)(10)].

Observe manufacturer cantilever limits, or if unavailable, a registered professional engineer's written limit [29cfr1926.1404(j)]. Keep component weights readily available [29cfr1926.1404(k)]. Components and configuration affecting capacity or safety follow manufacturer requirements (or written engineer approval if unavailable) or qualifying approved modifications; inspect after assembly [29cfr1926.1404(m)]. Remove and safely stow reusable shipping hardware [29cfr1926.1404(o)]. No jib during pile driving [29cfr1926.1404(p)].

Whenever outriggers or stabilizers are required or used, rules cover extension, floats, visibility and blocking; outriggers, except on locomotive cranes, must take equipment weight off wheels. Locomotive cranes have manufacturer-procedure rules [29cfr1926.1404(q)]. Rigging requires a qualified rigger, synthetic sling protection and compliance with sling manufacturer instructions and recommendations, alongside other applicable rigging standards [29cfr1926.1404(r)]. “(i) Protect the structural integrity of the equipment, and (ii) Prevent dangerous movement and collapse. (4) Verifying assist crane loads. When using an assist crane, the loads that will be imposed on the assist crane at each phase of assembly/disassembly must be verified in accordance with § 1926.1417(o)(3) before assembly/disassembly begins. (5) Boom and jib pick points. The point(s) of attachment of rigging to a boom (or boom sections or jib or jib sections) must be suitable for preventing structural damage and facilitating safe handling of these components.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. §1910.180 Crawler locomotive and truck cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.180(b)(3)]. Design: ANSI B30.5-1968 for new cranes from August 31, 1971; older cranes "should be modified" by February 15, 1972, subject to an exception [29cfr1910.180(b)(2)]. Maximum ratings (% of tipping): locomotive without outriggers, 85 (booms 60 feet or less, and over), with a 30,000 pound-feet minimum net stabilizing moment; locomotive, outriggers fully extended, 80; crawler without, 75, extended, 85; truck/wheel, without or extended, 85 [29cfr1910.180-table-1]. Locomotive rating track is within 1 percent grade [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(ii)(b)]. Account for wind, ground, tires, speeds and other stability factors [29cfr1910.180(c)(1)(iv)]. Keep the chart visible from your seat [29cfr1910.180(c)(2)].

Exceed rated load only for testing [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(i)]; tests stop at 110 percent [29cfr1910.180(e)(2)(ii)]. Structurally limited loads need weight known within ±10 percent [29cfr1910.180(h)(1)(ii)]. Sling loads; never wrap the hoist rope around them [29cfr1910.180(h)(2)]. Level, block, balance and control movement; no sideways dragging or riders [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)]. Test brakes by raising near-rated loads a few inches [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(viii)]. Use outriggers when load exceeds the no-outrigger rating [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(ix)]. Keep two full drum wraps [29cfr1910.180(h)(3)(x)]. Inspect new or altered cranes before use [29cfr1910.180(d)(1)]. Frequent: daily to monthly; periodic: 1 to 12 months or manufacturer's recommendation [29cfr1910.180(d)(2)]. Control maladjustment and air/hydraulic checks are daily [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)]. Hook criteria are cracks, throat over 15 percent excess, or twist over 10°; the sentence omits the action [29cfr1910.180(d)(3)(v)]. These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401].

Marine worksite means a construction worksite located in, on or above the water. Mobile crane means a lifting device incorporating a cable suspended latticed boom or hydraulic telescopic boom designed to be moved between operating locations by transport over the road. Moving point-to-point means the times during which an employee is in the process of going to or from a work station. Multi-purpose machine means a machine that is designed to be configured in various ways, at least one of which allows it to hoist (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.

§1910.184 Slings Inspect slings, fastenings and attachments daily before use, and during use as conditions warrant; a designated competent person does the daily check. Pull damaged or defective slings immediately [29cfr1910.184(d)]. Follow all safe practices on loading, rigging, identification and keeping clear; "Shock loading is prohibited." [29cfr1910.184(c)]. Five degrees or less from vertical may count as vertical [29cfr1910.184(b)].

Chain: thorough inspections at most 12 months apart [29cfr1910.184(e)(3)(i)]; proof test new, repaired or reconditioned slings before use [29cfr1910.184(e)(4)]. Remove permanently above 1000 degrees F; derate above 600 [29cfr1910.184(e)(6)]. Apply Table N-184-1 wear minimums (1⁄4-inch: 13⁄64) [29cfr1910.184(e)(8)] [29cfr1910.184-table-N-184-1]. Remove cracked or deformed components, and cracked hooks or hooks opened over 15 percent or twisted over 10 degrees [29cfr1910.184(e)(9)].

Wire rope: clear or circumferential minimums are 10, 40 or 96 diameters, by construction [29cfr1910.184(f)(2)]. Retire fiber-core slings exposed above 200 °F; for nonfiber core above 400 or below minus 60 °F, follow the manufacturer [29cfr1910.184(f)(3)]. Proof test welded attachments at twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(f)(4)(ii)]. Removal includes 10 random broken wires per lay or five in one strand per lay, one-third outer-wire diameter wear, and the 15-percent/10-degree hook limits, among other damage [29cfr1910.184(f)(5)].

Mesh: proof test at least 1 1/2 times capacity [29cfr1910.184(g)(5)]. Uncoated range is minus 20 to 550 °F; PVC or neoprene, zero to 200 °F [29cfr1910.184(g)(7)]. Removal limits include 25 per cent (abrasion), 15 (corrosion), 10 (slot depth or eye width) and 15 percent (handle-eye area) [29cfr1910.184(g)(9)].

Fiber rope: minus 20 to 180 °F, except wet frozen [29cfr1910.184(h)(2)]. Manila eye/short splices need three/six tucks; synthetic, four/eight. Rules also cover tails, 10-diameter clear length and 60-degree maximum eye angle [29cfr1910.184(h)(3)]. No repaired slings [29cfr1910.184(h)(6)].

Web: observe chemical restrictions [29cfr1910.184(i)(6)]; maximums are 180 °F (nylon, polyester) and 200 °F (polypropylene) [29cfr1910.184(i)(7)]. Proof test repairs to twice capacity [29cfr1910.184(i)(8)(ii)]. “(ii) Braided slings shall have a minimum clear length of wire rope 40 times the component rope diameter between the loops or end fittings. (iii) Cable laid grommets, strand laid grommets and endless slings shall have a minimum circumferential length of 96 times their body diameter. (3) Safe operating temperatures. Fiber core wire rope slings of all grades shall be permanently removed from service if they are exposed to temperatures in excess of 200 °F.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “These include, but are not limited to, the devices listed in § 1926.1416 (“listed operational aids”). Operational controls means levers, switches, pedals and other devices for controlling equipment operation. Operator means a person who is operating the equipment. Overhead and gantry cranes includes overhead/bridge cranes, semigantry, cantilever gantry, wall cranes, storage bridge cranes, launching gantry cranes, and similar equipment, irrespective of whether it travels on tracks, wheels, or other means.”

§1926.1432(b)(1) “(1) The multiple-crane/derrick lift must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (lift director).” §1926.1404(a)(1) “(1) Assembly/disassembly must be directed by a person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, or by a competent person who is assisted by one or more qualified persons (“A/D director”).” §1926.1432 Multiple-crane/derrick lifts—supplemental requirements These supplemental requirements apply to a crane/derrick operation in which more than one crane/derrick will be supporting the load. The operation must be planned before it begins [29cfr1926.1432(a)].

For the plan itself, a qualified person must develop it [29cfr1926.1432(a)(1)]. It must be designed "to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met" [29cfr1926.1432(a)(2)]. A decision point concerns engineering: where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided [29cfr1926.1432(a)(3)].

For implementation, the lift must be directed by a lift director, and there are two acceptable arrangements [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. The first is a single person who meets the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person. The second is a competent person "who is assisted by one or more qualified persons" [29cfr1926.1432(b)(1)]. Under the wording of that paragraph, a competent person who does not also meet the qualified person criteria needs that assistance to fit either arrangement.

The lift director must also review the plan in a meeting with all workers who will be involved with the operation [29cfr1926.1432(b)(2)]. “The planning must meet the following requirements: (1) The plan must be developed by a qualified person. (2) The plan must be designed to ensure that the requirements of this subpart are met. (3) Where the qualified person determines that engineering expertise is needed for the planning, the employer must ensure that it is provided. (b) Plan implementation. §1926.1414 Wire rope—selection and installation criteria Original and replacement rope must be selected and installed under this section. Replacement selection follows the rope manufacturer's, equipment manufacturer's, or a qualified person's recommendations [29cfr1926.1414(a)]. Rope must be compatible with safe equipment functioning [29cfr1926.1414(c)]. Non-rotation-resistant rope must meet ASME B30.5-2004 section 5-1.7.1, excluding paragraph (c) [29cfr1926.1414(b)(1)], or the performance option tied to rated capacity and § 1926.1413 inspections [29cfr1926.1414(b)(2)].

Rotation resistant types are Type I (at least 15 outer strands, at least three layers), Type II (at least 10, two or more layers) and Type III (no more than nine, two layers) [29cfr1926.1414(e)(1)]. The operating design factor floor for all is 3.5 [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(ii)]. Type I needs at least 5 unless both the rope and equipment manufacturers approve the factor in writing [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(iii)]. Types II and III below 5 are barred from duty cycle or repetitive lifts [29cfr1926.1414(e)(2)(i)]. For other lifts below 5, each operation requires a qualified person's inspection under § 1926.1413(a), with use only if no hazardous deficiencies are found; more than one broken wire in any one rope lay is a hazard [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(i)]. Operating manner and speed must minimize dynamic effects [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(ii)]. Record each such lift in the monthly and annual inspection documents; the qualified person considers prior uses before reuse [29cfr1926.1414(e)(3)(iii)].

For boom hoists, fiber core rope is allowed only on derricks [29cfr1926.1414(d)(1)]. Rotation resistant rope is allowed only where load hoists act as boom hoists for attachments such as luffing or boom and mast systems. Drum first-layer and all sheave pitch diameters must be at least 18 times nominal rope diameter, the system design factor at least five, and the other listed conditions met, including any power-controlled lowering system's capability [29cfr1926.1414(e)(4)(ii)].

Wedge socket clips attach only to the unloaded dead end, though purpose-designed dead-ending devices are permitted [29cfr1926.1414(f)]. Socket as the rope or fitting manufacturer specifies [29cfr1926.1414(g)]. Before cutting, seize both sides, following the rope manufacturer's length and number instructions [29cfr1926.1414(h)]. “(c) Wire rope must be compatible with the safe functioning of the equipment. (d) Boom hoist reeving. (1) Fiber core ropes must not be used for boom hoist reeving, except for derricks. (2) Rotation resistant ropes must be used for boom hoist reeving only where the requirements of paragraph (e)(4)(ii) of this section are met. (e) Rotation resistant ropes— (1) Definitions— (i) Type I rotation resistant wire rope (“Type I”). Type I rotation resistant rope is stranded rope constructed to have little or no tendency to rotate or, if guided, transmits little or no torque.”

§1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “if it is moveable up and down, it is referred to as a boom. Boom angle indicator means a device which measures the angle of the boom relative to horizontal. Boom hoist limiting device includes boom hoist disengaging device, boom hoist shut-off, boom hoist disconnect, boom hoist hydraulic relief, boom hoist kick-outs, automatic boom stop device, or derricking limiter. This type of device disengages boom hoist power when the boom reaches a predetermined operating angle. It also sets brakes or closes valves to prevent the boom from lowering after power is disengaged.”

§1910.179 Overhead and gantry cranes Only designated personnel operate [29cfr1910.179(b)(8)]. Stay within rated load except for tests [29cfr1910.179(n)(1)]; test loads are limited to 125 percent unless the manufacturer recommends otherwise [29cfr1910.179(k)(2)]. Each shift, try every upper hoist limit under no load, inching or slowly; immediately notify the appointed person of faults. Never use it as an operating control [29cfr1910.179(n)(4)].

Check rope, lines and hook position before hoisting; secure and balance loads; avoid sudden speed changes and obstructions. Side pulls need specific authorization. No movement with employees on load or hook. Avoid carrying loads over people, test brakes near rated load, keep two full drum wraps, stay at controls, and sound warnings when required. Multi-crane lifts need one qualified responsible person in charge [29cfr1910.179(n)(3)].

Frequent inspections run daily to monthly, periodic 1 to 12 months [29cfr1910.179(j)(1)(ii)]. Hooks and chains need daily visual and monthly certified checks; hook limits are over 15 percent excess throat opening or over 10° twist [29cfr1910.179(j)(2)]. Idle 1 to under 6 months requires frequent and idle-rope inspection; over 6 months, complete and idle-rope inspection; standby cranes, frequent and idle-rope inspection at least semi-annually [29cfr1910.179(j)(4)]. Running ropes need monthly certified inspection; ropes idle a month or more need appointed-person approval [29cfr1910.179(m)].

Before repair, position the crane, turn controllers off, lock the main or emergency switch open, post signs and protect against other cranes [29cfr1910.179(l)(2)(i)].

Equipment limits: ANSI B30.2.0-1967 design for new cranes from August 31, 1971 [29cfr1910.179(b)(2)]; clearances 3 inches overhead, 2 lateral, 3 around cabs; access gaps 12 inches (30 cm) maximum [29cfr1910.179(b)(6)(i)] [29cfr1910.179(c)]; footwalk headroom 48 inches, load design 50 pounds per square foot [29cfr1910.179(d)]; steppable guards support 200 pounds [29cfr1910.179(e)(6)(iii)]. Bumpers, subject to exceptions: bridge 3 ft/s/s at 20 percent rated speed, 40 percent energy capacity; trolley 4.7 at one-third [29cfr1910.179(e)]. Holding torque: 125 percent with nonmechanical control braking, 100 with mechanical, 100 each for two [29cfr1910.179(f)(2)(i)]. Foot force maximum 70 pounds; stopping feet equal 10 percent of full-load feet-per-minute speed [29cfr1910.179(f)(4)]. Voltage: control 600, pendant 150 AC/300 DC, cab-crane receptacle 300 [29cfr1910.179(g)]. Rope load per part: 20 percent breaking strength; retighten new-rope clips after one hour [29cfr1910.179(h)(2)]. “The bumpers shall be capable of stopping the crane (not including the lifted load) at an average rate of deceleration not to exceed 3 ft/s/s when traveling in either direction at 20 percent of the rated load speed.”

§1926.1437 Floating cranes/derricks and land cranes/derricks on barges This supplements the subpart for floating and barge-mounted cranes and derricks, excluding jacked barges fully supported by deployed jacks [29cfr1926.1437(a)]. Work area control applies except § 1926.1424(a)(2)(ii); use barriers, or signs plus equipment markings and employee training [29cfr1926.1437(c)]. § 1926.1425 doesn't apply [29cfr1926.1437(d)]. Add list/trim and house-lock devices, plus a wind indicator when a competent person finds wind relevant [29cfr1926.1437(e)]. Anti two-block applies only to personnel hoisting or hoisting over occupied cofferdams or shafts; listed work has load-weighing relief [29cfr1926.1437(f)]. Cab or no-cab information-access rules apply [29cfr1926.1437(g)].

Competent persons inspect the flotation each shift and monthly [29cfr1926.1437(h)(3)]. Annual external and four-year internal inspections require specified expertise; hazards remove the vessel from service, and flagged nonhazards are monitored [29cfr1926.1437(h)(4)] [29cfr1926.1437(h)(5)]. Document monthly, annual and four-year inspections; keep four-year records at least 4 years [29cfr1926.1437(h)(6)].

Diver work requires dedicated crane use until all divers return, continuous control attendance, tender sightline or electronic signals, and no-shift securing [29cfr1926.1437(j)]. Don't exceed vessel environmental, operating or transit limits [29cfr1926.1437(k)].

For permanent marine equipment, follow water charts and their parameters; charts consider minimum 40 mph wind [29cfr1926.1437(m)(1)]. List/trim maximums, in degrees, are 5 each at 25 tons or less, 7 over 25, and 10 for derricks [29cfr1926.1437-table-M1]. Stability: 60 mph with 2 ft freeboard at rated capacity or high boom/no load; 1 ft at capacity plus 25% [29cfr1926.1437-table-M2]; backward stability, high boom/no load/full back list, 90 mph [29cfr1926.1437-table-M3]. Employer-made equipment needs engineer-signed proof [29cfr1926.1437(m)(4)].

Land equipment needs expert derating [29cfr1926.1437(n)(2)]. Vessel list/trim cannot exceed the least of 5 degrees or the manufacturer's limit (qualified person's if unspecified), and must preserve above-water decks and a fully submerged bottom [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(i)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(4)]. Crane list/trim limits also apply [29cfr1926.1437(n)(3)(ii)]. Secure by attachment, corral, rails or centerline cable, except qualifying mobile auxiliaries under a plan [29cfr1926.1437(n)]. Both equipment categories have hull requirements [29cfr1926.1437(m)(5)] [29cfr1926.1437(n)(7)]. “| | Any rated capacity | 10 | 10 (3) The employer must ensure that the equipment is stable under the conditions specified in Tables M2 and M3 of this section. (Note: Freeboard is the vertical distance between the water line and the main deck of the vessel.) §1926.1401 Definitions These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].

For lowering, controlled load lowering uses the hoist drive motor rather than the load hoist brake. In free fall, only the brake regulates descent [29cfr1926.1401].

Near power lines, a dedicated spotter must meet § 1926.1428 and has the sole responsibility of watching separation and communicating with you so the minimum approach distance is not breached. A dedicated channel is assigned to "only one signal person and crane/derrick" or to a coordinated group. The employer controlling the communication system assigns it [29cfr1926.1401].

The fall zone extends beyond the area directly under the load to wherever suspended materials could foreseeably fall in an accident. Assembly/disassembly terms change for tower cranes to "erecting and climbing" and "dismantling." Any height increase is erection. Dismantling includes partial dismantling [29cfr1926.1401].

A multi-purpose machine is covered when configured with a winch pack, a jib with a hook, or a jib used with a winch, but not when configured with forks or tongs [29cfr1926.1401]. “Electrical contact occurs when a person, object, or equipment makes contact or comes in close proximity with an energized conductor or equipment that allows the passage of current. Employer-made equipment means floating cranes/derricks designed and built by an employer for the employer's own use. Encroachment is where any part of the crane, load line or load (including rigging and lifting accessories) breaches a minimum clearance distance that this subpart requires to be maintained from a power line. Equipment means equipment covered by this subpart.”

body.text: §1926.1401 Definitions

These definitions control how the subpart's terms are read [29cfr1926.1401]. "Include/including" and "Such as" introduce non-exhaustive examples, and "Up to" means "up to and including." Load covers the hoisted objects and load-attaching equipment, such as the load block, ropes and slings, whether the term refers to the objects or their weight. Rated capacity is the manufacturer's maximum working load under specified conditions, typically involving configuration, radius and boom length [29cfr1926.1401].

Know your devices. A load moment (rated capacity) indicator compares the lifting condition with rated capacity and shows the percentage in use. A limiter, once rated capacity is reached, cuts power to functions that can increase loading severity; functions that reduce it typically remain operational. A boom hoist limiting device disengages boom hoist power at a predetermined angle and prevents lowering afterward by setting brakes or closing valves. Range control devices are operator-set: one limits boom or jib tip movement, the other warns. Operational aids provide information or automatically take control of a function, including those listed in § 1926.1416 [29cfr1926.1401].
